The categorical (cat) model adds item classes to the spatial model:

  - distance to the last item (`rho_delta`),
  - direction relative to the last move (`rho_psi`),
  - absolute direction (`fourier_coef`),
  - a class-transition matrix (`b_v`) sets how likely the next item is to be the
same class as the last ("sticking") or a different one.

The multi-level version gives each person their own parameter values
(`u_*`) around the condition values, with between-person SDs
(`sigma_u_*`).

We simulate six people with known parameters, fit the model, and check it
recovers them.

Code: `cat.R`.

```{r}
#| include: false
knitr::read_chunk("cat.R")
```

```{r load}
```

## The transition matrix and the papers' parameters

The single-level cat example shows how `b_v` relates to the papers' class
weight $b_a$ and stick/switch rate $b_s$: with two classes they are the
same model. The multi-level models differ even then:

- each row's log-odds get their own per-person random effect,
  independently;
- on the papers' scale, that ties the between-person spreads of $b_a$ and
  $b_s$ together.

## Simulate

Six people, $K = 2$ conditions, 10 trials per person and condition, on an
8 $\times$ 8 grid with a quarter of cells empty and two item classes.
The conditions differ in every parameter:

- Condition *one* sticks with class 1 (rows 0.85/0.15 and 0.45/0.55:
  $b_a \approx 0.77$, $b_s \approx 0.97$), has weaker distance attraction
  (0.75), turns back ($-1$) and prefers the four cardinal directions;
- Condition *two* sticks with class 2 (rows 0.5/0.5 and 0.2/0.8:
  $b_a \approx -0.69$, $b_s \approx 0.69$), has stronger distance
  attraction (1.5), carries on (1) and prefers moving right.

Each trial's first selection has no previous item, so it is weighted by
class only, using the stationary distribution of each person's transition
matrix. Each person's values vary around the condition values: the
simulation draws each between-person SD from an exponential with rate
`sd_lambda` (a larger rate means less spread between people), then each
person's values.

```{r stimuli}
```


```{r fig-trial}
#| fig-cap: "One simulated trial from each condition: items (coloured by class) and selection order."
```

## Fit

We now fit the multi-level categorical version of FoMo to our simulated
data. Four chains of `r n_iter` warmup and `r n_iter` sampling iterations.

*Note*: by default some per-person effects are centred (`centred_params`,
see `prep_stan_list()`): distance and the class transitions. With only a
few trials per person that gives a funnel and many divergent transitions,
so here none are centred (`centred_params = "none"`). We checked this on
data simulated as on this page (six people, 10 trials per person and
condition), with two seeds, each dataset fitted both ways (4 chains of 500
warmup and 500 sampling iterations; recovery counts every simulation value,
per-person ones included):

| Seed | Centring | Divergent transitions | Largest R-hat | Smallest bulk ESS | Recovery | Time (min) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 65 | default | 29 | 1.014 | 206 | 236 of 240 | 18.5 |
| 65 | none | 0 | 1.011 | 605 | 237 of 240 | 32.8 |
| 101 | default | 101 | 1.030 | 113 | 235 of 240 | 10.8 |
| 101 | none | 2 | 1.012 | 374 | 233 of 240 | 15.7 |

With the default centring, the divergences and the worst R-hat and ESS all
come from the between-person SDs of the class transitions (`sigma_u_v`).
Without centring, there are none or a few, and every parameter mixes
better. Centring suits effects that each person's data pin down well,
which takes more data per person than this: on the real datasets (20-40
trials per person) the default works well. Even without centring, a few
divergent transitions can happen with this little data per person.

```{r fit_prep}
#| results: hide
```

## Diagnostics

Posterior medians and 97% HPDIs, the values the data were simulated from
(`true`, and whether each is `inside` its HPDI), and convergence (R-hat,
ESS), for the fixed effects and the between-person SDs (`sigma_u_*`).
Each person's values (`u_*`) are summarised in one row per parameter.
About one in 33 simulation values should fall outside its HPDI by chance;
with six people the SDs are hard to pin down. R-hat above 1.01, or a bulk
or tail ESS in the low hundreds, means the chains haven't mixed well
enough to trust the tails of the posterior. The summary's last line names
the worst parameter (random effects included); the table colours R-hat
and ESS green (good), orange (acceptable) or red (bad).

```{r fit-summary}
#| results: asis
```

Rank plots of the five worst-mixing parameters, judged by R-hat and ESS
together. Each histogram shows where one chain's draws rank among all the
draws: if the chains have mixed well, every chain's histogram is roughly
flat and they overlap.

```{r fig-traces}
#| fig-cap: "Rank plots of the five worst-mixing parameters, coloured green (good), orange (acceptable) or red (bad) by their R-hat and ESS."
```

`log_lik` is one value per trial, so loo leaves out a whole trial at a
time. A Pareto k above 0.7 marks a trial the fit leans on heavily, whose
loo estimate is unreliable. `check_high_pareto_k()` lists those trials,
worst first, with the person each belongs to (`z`).

```{r loo}
```

## Posterior

Where a posterior sits well inside its prior band, the data rather than
the prior set the estimate. A posterior pressed against the edge of its
band means the prior is doing some of the work.

```{r fig-post}
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Posterior densities by condition. Grey bands: prior HPDIs; dashed lines: simulation values."
```

Per-person estimates are pulled towards the condition value (shrinkage),
most for people whose own data say least. So a person's interval can
miss an extreme simulation value even when the condition values are
recovered.

```{r fig-person-spatial}
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Each person's $\\rho_\\delta$ and $\\rho_\\psi$: posterior intervals, simulation values (squares) and condition-level HPDIs (shaded)."
```

- Deterministic accuracy: how often the item the model judges most likely
is the one selected.
- Probability of the chosen item: the probability the
model gave the item that was selected, averaged over selections; it
credits the model for being nearly right, not only for top picks.
- Chance (1 / items left) rises through a trial as fewer items remain.
- The nearest-neighbour baseline always picks the closest remaining
item, so the gap above it is what the model adds to proximity alone.

```{r fig-accuracy}
#| fig-cap: "Accuracy of the model's predictions at each selection, with chance and nearest-neighbour baselines."
```

## Posterior predictive check

None of the trial statistics below is a model parameter, so reproducing
them tests whether the fitted model captures aspects of the behaviour it
was not fitted to directly. The model doesn't predict when a trial stops,
so each simulated trial keeps as many selections as the data have.
